title: Gold plated vs gold polished vs micro plated jewellery
description: Gold plated, gold polished and micro plated sound alike but mean different finishes. Learn what each term usually means and what to ask before buying.
intro: All three terms describe a gold-coloured layer over a cheaper base metal, but they are not the same thing. Gold plating usually means a real layer of gold bonded to the metal by electroplating. 'Gold polish' is a looser shop term that can mean anything from light plating to a gold-toned coating. 'Micro plated' usually refers to a finer, more controlled plating used on detailed pieces. Because none of these words are officially standardised in fashion jewellery, the smartest thing you can do is understand the general meaning and then ask the seller exactly what they mean.

sections.heading: Gold plating: the basic method
paragraphs: In electroplating, a finished piece of brass, copper or alloy is cleaned and dipped into a solution containing gold, and an electric current deposits a thin layer of gold on its surface. The thickness of this layer is what decides how long the colour lasts. It is measured in microns, which is why you may see sellers talk about 'micron gold plating' or the number of microns.

A thicker layer survives friction and sweat longer. A very thin 'flash' plating looks identical on day one but may start showing the base metal sooner, especially on edges and hooks that rub against skin and clothes.
Many pieces also get a clear anti-tarnish lacquer on top. This protective coat helps the colour last, but it can wear away too, so care matters even with good plating.

sections.heading: What 'gold polish' usually means
paragraphs: In Indian markets, 'gold polish' is used in a few different ways, which is exactly why it causes confusion. Some sellers use it as a casual synonym for gold plating. Others mean a thinner, cheaper finish, or a gold-coloured coating that is not a real gold layer at all. And when people say 'I got my jewellery polished', they often mean they had an old piece re-plated at a local shop.

The finish can look lovely, so there is nothing wrong with buying it. Just do not assume that 'gold polish' tells you anything about thickness or durability. Ask whether the piece is electroplated, and whether it has an anti-tarnish coat.

sections.heading: What micro plating usually means
paragraphs: Micro plating, sometimes written as micro gold plating, is a term you will see most often with American Diamond and CZ jewellery. It generally refers to a careful, fine plating process that coats the metal evenly, including tiny claws and grooves, without clogging the detail or dulling the stones.

Sellers often present micro plated pieces as longer-lasting and closer to the look of real gold. That can be true for well-made pieces, but as with every term here, the quality depends on the workshop, not the label.

sections.heading: Side by side, in simple terms
paragraphs: Here is a general way to think about the three, keeping in mind that individual sellers may use the words differently:
list: Gold plated: a real gold layer applied by electroplating. Durability depends on thickness and top coating.
Gold polished: a broad term. Could be plating, a thinner flash, or a gold-tone coating. Ask before you assume.
Micro plated: a fine, detailed plating, common on AD and CZ pieces, usually aimed at a more refined finish.
1 gram gold or forming gold: other market terms you may hear for gold-covered jewellery. Again, the method behind the name varies.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before you pay
paragraphs: A good seller will answer these clearly. If the answers are vague, treat that as information too.
list: What is the base metal: brass, copper or alloy?
Is the finish electroplated, and is there an anti-tarnish coating on top?
Is the back plated as well as the front?
Are the ear hooks or posts plated, or a different metal?
What is the return policy if the colour does not match the photos?

sections.heading: How to make any gold finish last longer
paragraphs: Whatever the label, the enemies are the same: sweat, water, perfume, lotion and rubbing. Put jewellery on last and take it off first. Wipe it with a soft dry cloth before putting it away, paying attention to the inside of necklaces and the backs of earrings where sweat collects. Store each piece in its own zip pouch so plated surfaces do not grind against each other.

When a favourite piece does start to fade, re-plating is often possible at a local jewellery repair shop, especially for brass-based pieces. For example, the [Kundan necklace sets](/women/necklaces) at Varaha use a brass base with gold plating, which is the kind of construction that usually takes re-plating well.

faq.q: Is gold polish the same as gold plating?
faq.a: Not always. Some sellers use the terms interchangeably, but gold polish can also mean a thinner finish or a gold-toned coating. Ask the seller.

faq.q: Is micro plated jewellery real gold?
faq.a: No. It is a base metal with a thin, fine gold layer on top, so it has the look of gold, not the value.

faq.q: How long does gold plating last?
faq.a: It depends on thickness, coating, how often you wear it and how you care for it. Gentle use and dry storage make a big difference.

faq.q: Can faded gold plated jewellery be re-plated?
faq.a: Often yes, especially pieces with a brass base. A local jewellery repair shop can usually advise you.
